drafts.title: Dinner is coming. What’s in the fridge?
drafts.body:
It’s 5:30. Everybody’s hungry. The fridge has eggs, rice and half a bag of carrots.

Try asking AI: “Give me three easy dinners with these ingredients. No extra shopping.”

Check the suggestions, then pick one.

What would you ask it to make with your leftovers?
bullets: Suggested everyday AI prompt using a hypothetical pantry. No personal experience or guaranteed result is claimed. Review suggestions for suitability.

drafts.title: Would an EV fit your Tuesday?
drafts.body:
School drop-off. Work. Groceries. Home.

That’s the EV question worth asking: can you charge where you park and cover your usual day?

A home charger isn’t an option for everybody. If you’d rely on public charging, check the stops and prices first.

What would work for you?
bullets: An opinion and practical charging checklist, not a claim that EVs fit every household. DOE describes home and public charging considerations. No personal ownership story is implied.

drafts.title: Same car. Different charging bill.
drafts.body:
An EV charging timer is worth a look before bed.

At 15¢ per kWh, 40 kWh costs $6. At 30¢, it’s $12. Same amount of electricity.

Those are example rates. Check your utility’s actual plan, including peak-hour costs for the rest of the house.

Does yours offer cheaper nights?
bullets: Illustrative arithmetic, not current local rates or promised savings: 40 × $0.15 = $6; 40 × $0.30 = $12. DOE confirms some utilities offer time-of-use rates. Compare the entire household tariff.

drafts.title: Your Medicare number is like a credit card number. AI fake texts are going after it right now (Tue ~11 AM or Wed ~8-9 AM)
drafts.window: Tue ~11 AM MT, or Wed ~8-9 AM.
drafts.angle: AI for normal people, scams, but a fresh angle (not the safe word again): fake texts and QR codes during open enrollment. One free rule, calm, no fear-mongering. OCR note: Strong. Save-and-forward post for 35-54 sons and daughters and their 55+ parents, with one simple rule.
bullets: Medicare open enrollment runs Oct 15 to Dec 7, 2026.
Experts warn AI makes fake texts look like real government messages; a Medicare number "is the equivalent of a credit card number" (WeAreIowa, Oct 15).
CMS: Medicare won't call you asking for your number. Hang up and call the number on the back of your card.
FCC: never join a plan over the phone unless YOU made the call. Real Medicare line: 1-800-633-4227.
His fill-ins: has a parent or friend gotten one [___].
drafts.body:
"$0 fix for the AI Medicare texts going around right now.

Open enrollment runs till December 7, and scammers are using AI to make texts that look exactly like the government sent them. Your Medicare number is basically a credit card number to these people.

Here's the rule: Medicare isn't going to text you or call you asking for it. Ever. Delete the text. Don't tap the link or scan the code. If you're worried, call 1-800-633-4227 yourself, or the number on the back of your card.

[Has your mom or dad gotten one of these? ___]

Who are you sending this to?"
drafts.pixel: 20 sec, phone in hand: "If you get a text about Medicare, here's the one thing to do."
drafts.target: A verified senior-money or consumer-protection creator posting open enrollment tips; reply with the one-rule version.

drafts.title: $942 million. What AI coding added to hospital bills, by one insurer's estimate. So use AI back (Wed ~8-9 AM)
drafts.angle: AI is on both sides of the medical bill now. Normal people can use it to read their bill and EOB. Honest, not hype, and it fits the AI-for-the-masses push. OCR note: OK. Big number and a useful step; OK to Strong if he adds a real line about checking his own bill. Keep it calm.
bullets: Blue Cross Blue Shield Association analysis (Blue Health Intelligence) estimated AI-assisted hospital coding added $942M in costs across 2024-2025 vs 2023. The American Hospital Association disputes that it shows inaccurate coding (AccountsRecovery.net, Oct 13).
Patients are using chatbots to compare bills with their Explanation of Benefits and flag duplicate charges.
More than 1 in 4 US adults owed medical debt in 2025 (Urban Institute / RWJF, as cited in coverage).
Caveat: AI can be wrong. Check every flagged line yourself before you dispute.
His fill-ins: ever caught a wrong charge [___], what he'd ask AI first [___].
drafts.body:
"$942 million. That's one insurer group's estimate of what AI-assisted coding added to hospital bills in two years. The hospitals say the coding is accurate. Either way, AI is already on your bill.

So use it back. Take a picture of your hospital bill and your Explanation of Benefits from the insurance company. Ask Grok or ChatGPT one plain question: what doesn't match?

It won't always be right, so check what it flags yourself before you call. But it reads the fine print in ten seconds, and most of us never read it at all.

[What I'd check first: ___]

Ever caught a wrong charge on a medical bill?"
